newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Breastfeeding a key issue in fight against AIDS.
newsitem.headline: Breastfeeding a key issue in fight against AIDS.

text.p: HIV-infected mothers face an agonising choice in some of the world's poorer areas -- risk transmitting AIDS to their babies by breastfeeding or use polluted water for bottle-feeding, a conference heard on Friday.

Experts recommend breastfeeding by healthy mothers, but it is known that milk from HIV-infected mothers also carries the virus, speakers told the conference on AIDS and women. Yet in many parts of the world bottle-feeding is too expensive or there is no clean water to make up the formula.
"Breastfeeding or bottle-feeding is the hot issue," Marie Laga of the Antwerp Institute for Tropical Medecine told the conference two days before World AIDS day. "It is a nightmare".

There are currently some 22 million people around the world -- of which 42 percent are women -- infected either with HIV, the virus which leads to AIDS, or with full-blown Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome. This includes 800,000 children.
Studies have found that around one-third of all babies born to HIV-infected women themselves become infected either before or during birth or through breastfeeding.
"The virus can be found in breastmilk, specifically in colostrum (pre-milk)," Diana Gibb of London's Institute of Child Health said. "Transmission occurs very early on."
An answer could be to tell infected mothers not to breastfeed. But in many places bottle-feeding is not an option.

It either costs too much or it is unsafe because you cannot drink the water, speakers said. In these many cases the mothers are advised to continue breastfeeding despite the fact they stand a strong chance of infecting their babies.
"There is no single answer," Sandra Wallman of Hull University in Britain, said.

In Europe the incidence of vertical transmission is between 15 and 20 percent, with similar levels in the United States. In Africa, where there are more than 14 million HIV or AIDS sufferers, it is between 25 and 39 percent, Gibb said.

Studies have shown that giving HIV-infected mothers the antiretrovirus drug AZT during pregnancy and birth, then giving it to the baby for six weeks after birth drastically cuts the rate of vertical transmission.

However, AZT is expensive and therefore only an option among the relatively wealthy, not the poor who tend to be the main sufferers either through prostitution, the weak social status of the women that allows men to refuse to wear condoms during intercourse or swapping dirty needles among drug users.
Figures from the United Nations anti-AIDS campaign show that what used to be thought of as a gay disease has now very much crossed the sexual barrier.
More than 70 percent of all adult HIV infections to date stem from heterosexual intercourse, with only about 10 percent from male homosexual intercourse, UNAIDS figures show.
Up to 10 percent of infections come from needle sharing among intravenous drug users, with up to five percent from tainted blood or blood products.
But the global distribution of the infection varies hugely.
UNAIDS has identified some 14 million HIV/AIDS sufferers in sub-Saharan Africa, with 4.8 million in South and South-East Asia and 1.3 million in Latin America.

There are 780,000 in North America, 470,000 in Western Europe, 270,000 in the Caribbean, 200,000 in North Africa and the Middle East, 35,000 in East Asia and the Pacific, 30,000 in Eastern Europe and Central Asia and 13,000 in Australasia.

HIV/AIDS prevalence among children is 35 times higher in the developing than in the developed world, yet the developing world can mostly not afford the treatments or even preventative measures that are available elsewhere.
